title: Stephen (Acts 6:8–7:60)
hookLine: the first to die for the faith forgives his killers as the stones fall
carry: lay not this sin to their charge
last: SUCH AS I HAVE, GIVE I THEE.

cards: An argument breaks out in Jerusalem: some widows are being left out of the daily food. The apostles ask the believers to choose seven people to run the tables.
The first name on the list is Stephen, a man, Acts says, full of faith and of the Holy Spirit.
A food organizer, but also a speaker, he gets into fierce debates in a Jerusalem synagogue, all of them Jews, arguing about Jesus, the temple and the law.
It ends with Stephen hauled before the council, where witnesses Acts calls false swear he's been speaking against the holy place.

teach.h: A HISTORY, TOLD TO THE COUNCIL.
teach.b: Stephen answers with a long speech: the history of his people, from Abraham to Moses to the temple, and in it God keeps meeting them far from any temple, in Mesopotamia, in Egypt, in the wilderness.
By the end the room is furious. Stephen looks up and says he sees heaven opened, and Jesus standing at God's right hand. They cover their ears, drag him outside the city, and stone him.
While the stones fall, he prays two things.
"Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Then, kneeling, loudly: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Sound familiar?

On the cross, in Luke's Gospel, Jesus prays, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do," and then commits his spirit into his Father's hands. Luke tells Stephen's death as an echo of his teacher's.
Martyr comes from the Greek martys, which first meant simply a witness, someone who tells a court what they saw.
Stephen is remembered as the first Christian martyr, and over time the word changed, until it meant a witness who dies rather than take back what they saw.
To be clear: this was a bitter quarrel among Jews, Stephen and the believers around him included, not a story about one people against another.

teach.h: COATS AT THE FEET OF SAUL.
teach.b: And a quiet detail at the edge of the scene: the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul.

teach.h: LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.
teach.b: Hold on to that name. Church tradition keeps Stephen's feast just after Christmas.

how: Christians honor Stephen as the first martyr, with a feast day on December 26 in Western churches and December 27 in many Orthodox churches. His dying prayer of forgiveness is often read alongside Jesus's words from the cross.

o: a saint known for working miracles in life
at first a witness; later one who dies for it
a judge who rules on church quarrels

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: chosen to run the daily food
the coats were laid at his feet

s: martyr first meant someone who dies for a cause
martys meant a witness, someone who tells what they saw. the dying meaning came later.
Stephen was one of the twelve apostles
he was one of the seven chosen to run the daily food for widows.
Stephen's last words echo Jesus's words on the cross
Luke tells both: a spirit committed to God, and forgiveness for those doing the killing.

games.q: you're Stephen. the stones are falling. you have breath for one more sentence. what is it?
o: a curse on the ones throwing.
a final defense of your speech.
a prayer that this sin not be held against them.
games.why: he kneels and cries out: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. then, Luke says, he fell asleep.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has hurt you, not the biggest wound, one you can hold for two minutes.

You don't have to tell them or say it was fine; Stephen didn't, he asked that it not be held against them, so see if you can let go of the charge, even a little. If you pray, use his words; if not, just loosen your grip.

wordCard.voice: Martyr. From the Greek martys, a witness. Stephen, remembered as the first, who forgave as he died.

orig.note: Greek: a witness, someone who testifies to what they saw. Later, one who dies for that witness.
